title: 1. Der, Die, Das & Gender Clues
summary: German nouns have three genders: Masculine (der), Feminine (die), and Neuter (das). Plural nouns always use 'die'.

rules.label: Der (Masculine)
rules.tip: Male people/animals, days, months, seasons, and nouns ending in -er, -ling, -or, -ismus (der Sommer, der Montag, der Lehrer).

rules.label: Die (Feminine)
rules.tip: Female people/animals, and nouns ending in -ung, -heit, -keit, -schaft, -tion, -tät, -ei (die Zeitung, die Freiheit, die Bäckerei).

rules.label: Das (Neuter)
rules.tip: Diminutives ending in -chen, -lein, infinitive nouns, and endings in -ment, -um, -tum (das Mädchen, das Brötchen, das Essen, das Museum).

rules.label: Die (Plural)
rules.tip: All plural nouns use 'die' in the nominative case regardless of their original singular gender!

fritz_tip: Look at the ending of the word! 99% of words ending in -ung, -heit, -keit, and -schaft are DIE. Words ending in -chen or -lein are always DAS (even das Mädchen)! 🦊💡

quiz.q: What is the article for 'Zeitung' (newspaper)?
quiz.hint: Words ending in -ung are always feminine!

quiz.q: What is the article for 'Mädchen' (girl)?
quiz.hint: The diminutive ending -chen always makes a noun neuter!

quiz.q: Which article do all plural nouns take in Nominative?
quiz.hint: Plural always takes 'die' in Nominative.

title: 2. Cases: Nominative vs. Accusative
summary: The Nominative case marks the SUBJECT (who does the action). The Accusative case marks the DIRECT OBJECT (who/what receives the action).

rules.label: The Magic Shift
rules.tip: ONLY the masculine gender changes in Accusative: der -> den, ein -> einen, kein -> keinen. Feminine, Neuter, and Plural do not change!

rules.label: Subject (Wer/Was?)
rules.tip: Der Mann trinkt einen Kaffee. -> 'Der Mann' is the subject (Nominative).

rules.label: Direct Object (Wen/Was?)
rules.tip: Er trinkt den Kaffee. -> 'den Kaffee' is the direct object (Accusative).

rules.label: Fixed Accusative Prepositions
rules.tip: bis, durch, für, gegen, ohne, um (Mnemonic: DOGFU / BDFGOU). These prepositions ALWAYS require Accusative!

fritz_tip: Remember: Only the masculine gets the 'N' in Accusative! 'Ich habe EINEN Hund (m), EINE Katze (f), EIN Auto (n)'. 🦊🐶

quiz.q: Fill in the blank: 'Ich kaufe _____ Apfel (m)'.
quiz.hint: Apfel is masculine and is the direct object: ein -> einen.

quiz.q: Which preposition ALWAYS takes the Accusative case?
quiz.hint: 'für' is always accusative (Das ist für dich!).

quiz.q: What happens to feminine nouns ('die Tasche') in Accusative?
quiz.hint: Feminine and Neuter never change between Nominative and Accusative.

title: 3. Dative Case Basics
summary: The Dative case marks the INDIRECT OBJECT (to whom / for whom) and is required after key everyday prepositions.

rules.label: Dative Article Shifts
rules.tip: der -> dem, das -> dem, die -> der, die (pl) -> den + n on the noun!

rules.label: Fixed Dative Prepositions
rules.tip: aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu (Sing to the melody of Blue Danube: aus-bei-mit, nach-seit-von-zu!).

rules.label: Common Dative Verbs
rules.tip: helfen (hilf mir!), danken (ich danke dir), gefallen (das gefällt mir), schmecken (das schmeckt mir).

fritz_tip: Sing the magic rhyme: 'Aus, bei, mit, nach, seit, von, zu — immer mit dem Dativ, du!' 🎶🦊

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Ich fahre mit _____ Bus (m)'.
quiz.hint: 'mit' requires Dative, so 'der' becomes 'dem'.

quiz.q: What does feminine 'die' turn into in Dative?
quiz.hint: Feminine 'die' flips to 'der' in the Dative case.

quiz.q: Which verb always takes a Dative object?
quiz.hint: 'helfen' takes Dative: 'Ich helfe dir'.

title: 4. Present Tense Verb Conjugation
summary: German verbs change their endings based on the subject pronoun: -e, -st, -t, -en, -t, -en.

rules.label: Regular Endings
rules.tip: ich -e | du -st | er/sie/es -t | wir -en | ihr -t | sie/Sie -en.

rules.label: Vowel Changers (du / er)
rules.tip: e -> i/ie (sprechen -> du sprichst, lesen -> er liest); a -> ä (fahren -> du fährst, schlafen -> er schläft).

rules.label: Verbs ending in -t / -d
rules.tip: Add an extra 'e' for pronunciation: arbeiten -> du arbeitest, er arbeitet.

fritz_tip: Remember the formula: 'E - ST - T - EN - T - EN'. Just drop the -en from the infinitive and snap on the matching ending! 🦊✨

quiz.q: Conjugate: 'Du _____ (sprechen) sehr gut Deutsch.'
quiz.hint: 'sprechen' has an e -> i vowel change for 'du' and 'er/sie/es'.

quiz.q: Conjugate: 'Er _____ (fahren) mit dem Zug.'
quiz.hint: 'fahren' takes an umlaut (ä) in the 3rd person singular.

quiz.q: What is the ending for 'wir' (we)?
quiz.hint: 'wir' always takes the '-en' ending (identical to the infinitive).

title: 5. The Big Three: Sein, Haben & Werden
summary: These three irregular auxiliary verbs are the absolute backbone of German conversation and future/past tenses.

rules.label: sein (to be)
rules.tip: Essential for identity, adjectives, professions, and location: 'Ich bin glücklich'.

rules.label: haben (to have)
rules.tip: Expresses possession and many idioms: 'Ich habe Hunger/Durst/Zeit'.

rules.label: werden (to become)
rules.tip: Used for changes of state and future tense: 'Es wird kalt'.

fritz_tip: Watch out for 'ihr seid' (you all are) vs. 'sie sind' (they are). They are easy to mix up! 🦊

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Wir _____ zwei Brüder.'
quiz.hint: Having family members uses 'haben'.

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Wie alt _____ du?'
quiz.hint: In German, you 'are' your age (sein), you don't 'have' it.

quiz.q: What is 'ihr' for the verb 'sein'?
quiz.hint: 'ihr seid' is the 2nd person plural form.

title: 6. Modal Verbs & The Sentence Bracket
summary: Modal verbs express ability, necessity, or desire. They send the main infinitive verb to the end of the sentence!

rules.label: können (can / able)
rules.tip: ich kann, du kannst, er kann, wir können

rules.label: müssen (must / have to)
rules.tip: ich muss, du musst, er muss, wir müssen

rules.label: wollen (want to)
rules.tip: ich will, du willst, er will, wir wollen

rules.label: möchten (would like)
rules.tip: ich möchte, du möchtest, er möchte, wir möchten

rules.label: dürfen (may / allowed)
rules.tip: ich darf, du darfst, er darf, wir dürfen

rules.label: sollen (should / ought)
rules.tip: ich soll, du sollst, er soll, wir sollen

fritz_tip: Notice that 'ich' and 'er/sie/es' have the EXACT same form with all modal verbs: 'ich kann' = 'er kann'! 🦊🎉

quiz.q: Where does the second verb go when using a modal verb?
options: At the very end of the sentence
quiz.hint: The main verb in infinitive form closes the bracket at the very end.

quiz.q: Conjugate: 'Er _____ (können) sehr schnell laufen.'
quiz.hint: 3rd person singular of können is 'kann' (no -t ending!).

quiz.q: Which modal verb expresses 'permission'?
quiz.hint: 'dürfen' means to be allowed / permitted.

title: 7. Word Order & The V2 Golden Rule
summary: In main clauses, the conjugated verb ALWAYS occupies the 2nd position. Even if you start with time or place!

rules.label: Standard SVO
rules.tip: [Position 1: Subject] + [Position 2: VERB] + [Rest]. Example: 'Ich lerne heute Deutsch.'

rules.label: Inversion (Time first)
rules.tip: [Position 1: Time/Place] + [Position 2: VERB] + [Position 3: Subject]. Example: 'Heute lerne ich Deutsch.'

rules.label: Questions
rules.tip: Yes/No questions put Verb in Position 1: 'Lernst du Deutsch?' W-questions put W-word in Pos 1, Verb in Pos 2: 'Wo lernst du Deutsch?'

fritz_tip: Position 2 does NOT mean the second word — it means the second grammatical block! 'Meine liebe Oma [1] kocht [2] die Suppe.' 🦊🍲

quiz.q: What happens if a sentence starts with 'Gestern' (Yesterday)?
quiz.hint: The verb MUST stay in Position 2: 'Gestern ging ich...'.

quiz.q: Which sentence has correct word order?
quiz.hint: Pos 1: Heute, Pos 2: fahre, Pos 3: ich.

quiz.q: Where does the verb sit in a Yes/No question?
quiz.hint: 'Kommst du morgen?' -> Verb is in Position 1.

title: 8. Negation: Nicht vs. Kein
summary: Never mix them up: use 'kein' for nouns with indefinite or zero articles, and 'nicht' for verbs, adjectives, and specific nouns.

rules.label: When to use KEIN
rules.tip: Replaces 'ein' or zero-article nouns: 'Ich habe EIN Auto' -> 'Ich habe KEIN Auto'. 'Ich habe Zeit' -> 'Ich habe KEINE Zeit'.

rules.label: When to use NICHT
rules.tip: Negates verbs, adjectives, adverbs, pronouns, and nouns with definite articles ('der/die/das'): 'Ich schlafe NICHT', 'Das ist NICHT gut', 'Ich kenne DEN Mann NICHT'.

rules.label: Doch!
rules.tip: If someone asks a negative question ('Kommst du nicht?') and you want to say yes, use 'DOCH!' instead of 'Ja'.

fritz_tip: If you could say 'no/not any' in English, use 'kein'. For everything else, use 'nicht'! 🦊⛔

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Ich habe _____ Zeit.' (Zeit is feminine, zero article)
quiz.hint: Negating a zero-article feminine noun takes 'keine'.

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Das Essen ist _____ teuer.'
quiz.hint: Negating an adjective ('teuer') takes 'nicht'.

quiz.q: Someone asks: 'Hast du keinen Hunger?' You are very hungry. You answer:
quiz.hint: 'Doch' contradicts a negative question.

title: 9. Common Prepositions & Cases
summary: Prepositions dictate the case of the noun that follows them. Master the essential A1 prepositions!

rules.label: Dative Prepositions
rules.tip: aus (from), bei (at/with), mit (with), nach (after/to), seit (since), von (from/of), zu (to). ALWAYS Dative!

rules.label: Accusative Prepositions
rules.tip: bis (until), durch (through), für (for), gegen (against/around), ohne (without), um (at/around). ALWAYS Accusative!

rules.label: Contractions
rules.tip: in + dem = im | an + dem = am | zu + dem = zum | zu + der = zur | bei + dem = beim | für + das = fürs.

fritz_tip: Remember: 'zum' = zu dem (masc/neut), 'zur' = zu der (fem). 'Ich gehe zum Arzt, aber zur Bank!' 🦊🏦

quiz.q: Fill in: 'Ein Kaffee _____ (without) Milch bitte.'
quiz.hint: 'ohne' means without.

quiz.q: What is the contraction for 'in dem'?
quiz.hint: 'in + dem' contracts to 'im'.

quiz.q: Which preposition means 'since' and takes Dative?
quiz.hint: 'seit' means since / for a period of time: 'seit einem Jahr'.

title: 10. Plural Patterns & Noun Endings
summary: Unlike English (-s), German has 5 main plural patterns: -e, -(e)n, -er, -s, and no ending (often with umlauts).

rules.label: Pattern 1: -e (often with Umlaut)
rules.tip: Common for masculine & neuter nouns: der Tisch -> die Tische, der Baum -> die Bäume.

rules.label: Pattern 2: -(e)n
rules.tip: Standard for ~90% of feminine nouns: die Frau -> die Frauen, die Lampe -> die Lampen.

rules.label: Pattern 3: -er (usually with Umlaut)
rules.tip: Mostly short neuter nouns: das Kind -> die Kinder, das Buch -> die Bücher, das Bild -> die Bilder.

rules.label: Pattern 4: -s
rules.tip: Foreign loanwords and abbreviations: das Auto -> die Autos, das Sofa -> die Sofas, das Handy -> die Handys.

rules.label: Pattern 5: No ending (or just Umlaut)
rules.tip: Nouns ending in -el, -en, -er: der Lehrer -> die Lehrer, der Apfel -> die Äpfel, der Computer -> die Computer.

fritz_tip: Whenever you learn a German noun, always learn it with its article AND its plural: 'der Tisch, die Tische'! 🦊📚

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'das Buch'?
quiz.hint: Das Buch takes an umlaut and -er: die Bücher.

quiz.q: What is the plural ending for most feminine nouns ending in -ung?
quiz.hint: die Zeitung -> die Zeitungen.

quiz.q: What is the plural of 'das Auto'?
quiz.hint: Loanwords usually take -s.
